data.title: Broadcom CEO dismisses AI slowdown concerns, stands by long-term revenue goals
data.description:
Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan dismissed fears that a potential slowdown in frontier AI model development would impact the company, telling CNBC that the chipmaker remains committed to its long-term revenue targets.

Tan’s comments came as investors were rattled by Anthropic (ANTHRO) CEO Dario Amodei’s weekend essay advocating for a moderation in the pace of model development. Amodei’s message, which received support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, prompted investors in AI infrastructure providers to reconsider their expectations for compute demand during Monday’s session.

Shares of Broadcom — whose custom-chip business counts Anthropic as one of its most important customers — fell 4.8%. A broad basket of chip stocks, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOX), fell 5.6%. The stocks of companies selling other data-center components were also hit hard.

“No, not in the least,” Tan said, when Jim Cramer asked whether anything in the AI slowdown debate has caused him to reconsider Broadcom’s fiscal 2027 and 2028 AI semiconductor forecasts. “We see the demand for compute infrastructure, for AI development or AI frontier models, and inference for the products that they feed to the world, as continuing to be very strong and, I believe, very durable.”

Tan also said Anthropic is on track to become Broadcom’s largest custom chip customer in 2027 and sustain that designation in 2028 — illustrating why Broadcom (AVGO) investors are so sensitive to Amodei’s commentary. Google has historically been considered Broadcom’s biggest custom customer, co-designing Google’s (GOOG) (GOOGL) tensor processing units.

In Monday’s CNBC interview, Tan was particularly optimistic about demand for inference, the day-to-day usage of AI models after they’ve been trained.

“I don’t know about training, but when you want to productize inference, I see it continuing to be very, very strong,” Tan said.

data.title: China retail sales miss expectations, while urban unemployment hits 5.3%
data.description:
• China’s retail sales growth slowed to 0.4% Y/Y in August 2026 from 0.6% in July, missing market expectations of 0.8%.
  • Auto sales fell 18.5%, while furniture, building materials, and gold and silver jewelry sales declined 7.9%, 11.8%, and 17.5%, respectively. Excluding autos, retail sales grew 2.5%.
  • Meanwhile, China’s surveyed urban unemployment rate rose to 5.3% from 5.2% in July, above the 5.2% expected and the highest since March. The rate among migrant workers increased to 5.2% from 5.1%.
  • From January to August, retail sales rose 1.1% year-on-year, while the average urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2%, unchanged from the first seven months.

data.title: EPA to roll back Biden-era limits on power plant emissions
data.description:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Monday it will repeal some carbon dioxide emission rules for power plants, the latest step in the Trump administration's broader effort to curb the agency's role in regulating climate change.

Under the final rule announced at the G-20 summit for energy ministers in Houston, the EPA is ending a Biden-era mandate requiring existing and future fossil fuel-fired power plants to dramatically curb their emissions in the coming decades through the use of specific technologies, including carbon capture and storage.

The EPA also proposed a new rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically are a significant source of air pollution, effectively a separate endangerment finding for power plants under the Clean Air Act after the agency acted in February to rescind the Obama-era endangerment finding, which classifies six greenhouse gases as a threat to public health and welfare.

The administration's rule changes earlier this year focused on the auto sector and tailpipe emissions, not the power industry.

"Today's proposal states the Clean Air Act does not give us the authority to regulate power plant emissions based on climate change," EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said at the G-20 meeting. "At EPA, we follow a very simple principle: If Congress didn't authorize it, EPA shouldn't be doing it."

Energy industry groups celebrated the rollback, while environmentalists and some former EPA officials criticized the repeal and warned that its economic and environmental fallout could be significant.

data.title: Chevron CEO Wirth, other U.S. oil executives warn global fuel crisis has arrived
data.description:
Trump administration officials have said the current oil market disruption is temporary, but Chevron's (CVX) Mike Wirth and other industry executives are warning global supplies are running low, with no respite in sight.

Commercial fuel stocks around the world have been depleting for more than six months, and strategic crude reserves cannot be tapped much further, oil executives say, after attacks last week shut down a crucial crude pipeline in Saudi Arabia that bypassed the Strait of Hormuz, stranding an estimated 2.5M bbl/day at least from an already tight global oil market.

"All these mechanisms helped to mitigate the price and supply risk," Chevron (CVX) CEO Mike Wirth said Friday at an energy conference in Austin, Texas, according to The Wall Street Journal. "Those have largely now played out, and we don't have nearly the buffers in the system that we did when [the Middle East war] began."

"It's harder ​to envision a scenario where prices soften and quickly," Wirth said. "I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months."

U.S. retail diesel prices have skyrocketed to a record $6.23/gal, and gasoline prices, which had slipped below $4 during the summer, have bounced to $4.32/gal, and WSJ reported that some CEOs and energy advisers are growing alarmed as the Middle East conflict has picked up again, with ships and energy infrastructure being targeted in both directions.

"The advantage in most negotiations usually goes to the side that has time on their side and is willing to be patient," and Iran is "willing to suffer," Quantum Capital Group CEO Wil VanLoh said at the Austin conference. "Their people have already suffered a lot for many decades."

Analysts say China is in part helping to exacerbate the global supply pinch, resuming bigger purchases from international suppliers after relying for months on its own stockpiles of crude for nearly half of its daily consumption, which had provided a reprieve for oil markets.

Crude oil futures settled higher Monday on mounting worries about energy supplies following new ‌strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and attacks on ships in the Middle East.

But prices eased off early highs, led by diesel, after President Trump said Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop attacks on each other's energy facilities, although neither country has independently said they are holding to the deal.

Ukraine President Zelenskyy said his country would be willing to suspend its strikes "if our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes... Ukraine is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement."

Front-month Nymex crude (CL1:COM) for October delivery gained 1.3% to $101.39/bbl, front-month Brent crude (CO1:COM) for November delivery added 1% to $105.68/bbl, and front-month Nymex October natural gas (NG1:COM) climbed 2.3% to $2.896/MMBtu.

data.title: Radiant Logistics signals $200M credit facility through 2031 while pursuing acquisitions and buybacks
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Radiant Logistics (RLGT) Q4 2026

Management View

  • CEO Bohn Crain framed Q4 as a broad-based improvement, saying, “We are pleased to report another quarter of solid financial results, delivering $10.4 million in adjusted EBITDA for our fourth fiscal quarter ended June 30, 2026,” and added that results showed “revenues up 18.5%… adjusted net income up 34.5% and adjusted EBITDA up 31.6%… and adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 240 basis points” versus the prior-year quarter.

  • Crain tied sequential momentum to domestic and international execution, stating, “Our quarter-over-quarter improvement was driven principally by our U.S. forwarding operations,” and citing “notable strength in our international airfreight operations,” while also positioning domestic cycle indicators as supportive: “Spot rates, tender rejections, and other cyclical indicators moved higher through the spring and carried into our fourth quarter.”

  • On product and go-to-market expansion, Crain highlighted increased adoption of the Navegate platform, saying, “one of our enterprise customers now actively managing over 1,400 vendors using the platform,” and announced a new growth channel: “we… launch[ed] a new independent agent program at Radiant Road & Rail.”

  • On balance sheet capacity and capital deployment, Crain said, “In August of 2026, we completed an amended and restated $200 million senior credit facility extending its maturity to 2031, expanding our acquisition focused accordion to $100 million and improving our pricing terms,” and emphasized, “we enter fiscal 2027 with no net debt.”

  • CFO Todd Macomber said, “For the 3 months ended June 30, 2026, we reported net income attributable to Radiant Logistics of $7.517 million on $261.4 million of revenues or $0.16 per basic and $0.15 per fully diluted share,” and added, “For adjusted EBITDA, we reported $10.362 million for the 3 months ended June 30, 2026.”

Outlook

  • Management did not provide formal EPS or revenue guidance in the prepared remarks; during Q&A, Crain described expectations for domestic brokerage and intermodal as improving and timing-driven, saying the market evolution “didn't start happening until late May, early June,” and, “we expect that to… continue to manifest… into… our quarter ended September and then on into subsequent quarters.”

  • On forward-looking demand drivers tied to trade complexity, Crain said escalating U.S.-Canada tariff actions “add a further layer of complexity,” and, “we expect this cross-border dynamic to remain a source of demand for our customs brokerage and compliance capabilities.”

  • Analyst-estimate comparisons were not included because the provided estimates data did not use the required quarter format (Q1–Q4).

Financial Results

  • Macomber reported Q4 profitability and revenue figures, stating, “For the 3 months ended June 30, 2026, we reported net income… of $7.517 million on $261.4 million of revenues,” and contrasted the prior-year quarter as “$4.907 million on $220.6 million of revenue.”

  • Macomber highlighted full-year earnings and revenue, saying, “For the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, we reported net income… of $18.786 million on $934.4 million of revenues,” compared with “$17.291 million on $902.7 million of revenues” for the prior year.

  • Macomber described a divergence between GAAP and adjusted full-year trends, stating, “For adjusted net income, we reported $25.253 million… compared to… $30.944 million,” and, “For adjusted EBITDA, we reported $36.684 million… compared to… $38.756 million.”

Q&A

  • Ryan Meyers, Lake Street Capital Markets: asked when improving domestic indicators would show up more meaningfully; CEO Crain said the comments were “pointed directly at… over-the-road truck brokerage… and… intermodal,” adding, “we really… only have 1 month of the good news… in our fiscal year-end results,” and expects improvement to “continue to manifest… into… our quarter ended September.”

  • Ryan Meyers, Lake Street Capital Markets: asked about fuel-cost pass-through; CEO Crain responded, “Generally speaking, fuel is a pass-through,” with “modest lags,” but, “we're able to pass those increasing fuel cost onto the customers relatively quickly.”

  • Elliot Alper (for Jason Seidl), TD Cowen: asked how structural the shifts are and what to expect for forwarding; CEO Crain said “most all of our businesses are actually kind of heading up into the right,” while cautioning, “who knows based upon trade policy… and what's going to happen in the Middle East.”

  • Elliot Alper (for Jason Seidl), TD Cowen: asked about airfreight pull-forward and disaster relief sizing; CEO Crain said, “we don't want to get into too much detail… for competitive reasons but it was certainly meaningful,” and added, “even without it, we still would have been up year-over-year.”

  • Elliot Alper (for Jason Seidl), TD Cowen: asked how Navegate will be priced and impact margins; CEO Crain said some customers want the cost embedded while others want separate billing, noting, “in other cases and more often the case, it's embedded as part of our transportation margin,” and emphasized, “I don't necessarily think of it as more margin… I think of it as winning more customers.”

  • Jeffrey Kauffman, Citizens JMP Securities: asked how to think about FY2027 growth given Q4 volatility; CEO Crain said, “we like to underpromise and overdeliver,” and urged focus on gross margin dollars because it “kind of neutralizes fuel,” while CFO Macomber added, “our organic was up about 8%,” and, “it's definitely at a stronger trend than what we've been seeing in the past.”

  • Jeffrey Kauffman, Citizens JMP Securities: asked about Q4 tax-rate dynamics; CFO Macomber said, “That was the One Big Beautiful Bill,” which allowed the company to take items “previously capitalized as far as internal software,” describing it as “a true-up… in the Q4.”

  • Jeffrey Kauffman, Citizens JMP Securities: asked about “Montgomery” and broker carrier selection risk; CEO Crain said the company has “a well-documented defined carrier vetting process,” and added, “We're not immune so we're taking it very seriously.”

  • Michael Vermut, Newland Capital Management: asked about enterprise pipeline and multi-year Navegate impact; CEO Crain said, “I don't have a crisp answer,” but highlighted vendor-led inbound interest and said, “we hope to activate current and prospective customers on to the Navegate platform.”

  • Michael Vermut, Newland Capital Management: asked about data center exposure and M&A appetite; CEO Crain said data centers are “not a driver” but the company has “exposure,” and on acquisitions, “there were more CIMs flying around,” adding, “we've got a lot of dry powder,” and argued “a path to practically double our EBITDA within our existing capital structure.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, with repeated acknowledgement of performance and probing on sustainability, including “Nice results in the quarter,” “congratulations on a real solid quarter,” and questions focused on durability of market shifts, fuel pass-through, tax-rate drivers, and brokerage liability exposure.

  • Management’s tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and remained measured in Q&A; CEO Crain used cautious qualifiers like “we believe” and “time will tell,” while also projecting confidence on domestic trends, saying, “I think it's going to continue for some time,” and reiterating discipline on M&A: “we expect to remain very disciplined in our approach.”

  • Versus the prior quarter, management kept the “not fully reflected” phrasing on domestic recovery but sounded more anchored in near-term timing, moving from Q3’s “approaching a genuine inflection point” to Q4’s view that the pivot began “late May, early June,” with more emphasis on agent growth (Road & Rail) and credit-facility upgrades.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q4 introduced new, concrete execution markers versus Q3: Crain disclosed an enterprise Navegate usage metric (“over 1,400 vendors”), described an airfreight lift tied to “disaster relief,” and announced the “new independent agent program at Radiant Road & Rail,” while Q3 placed relatively more emphasis on “Ray, our first AI-powered agent.”

  • Capital structure messaging sharpened in Q4: Crain detailed the amended facility (“$200 million… maturity to 2031… accordion to $100 million”) and reiterated “no net debt,” while Q3 emphasized being “essentially debt-free on a net basis relative to our $200 million credit facility.”

  • Analyst focus broadened in Q4 to include brokerage legal/process risk (“Montgomery”), tax rate drivers, and explicit questions on modeling organic growth; Q3 questions leaned more toward repricing opportunity and whether Navegate/Ray would be broken out with KPIs.

Risks and Concerns

  • Crain cited geopolitical and trade-policy uncertainty as ongoing variables, saying, “who knows based upon trade policy… and what's going to happen in the Middle East,” and described ocean routing disruption from “closure of the Strait of Hormuz and continued Houthi activity.”

  • On brokerage risk controls, Crain said the company must follow “a well-documented defined carrier vetting process,” adding, “we're taking it very seriously,” indicating process adherence as the key mitigation.

  • On visibility into Navegate monetization, Crain described customer preference variability, stating some want the tech “embedded” and others billed separately, and repeatedly cautioned, “I don't have a crisp answer,” on pipeline timing.

Final Takeaway

Radiant’s management described Q4 as a step-up quarter led by U.S. forwarding and international airfreight, while positioning domestic truck brokerage and intermodal as entering a more constructive rate-and-capacity setup that began late in the quarter and is expected to carry into early fiscal 2027. The call added new specifics around Navegate adoption (an enterprise account managing over 1,400 vendors), a new independent agent program at Road & Rail, and expanded financial flexibility via an amended $200 million credit facility extended to 2031 with a $100 million accordion, alongside reiterated plans for disciplined acquisitions and potential buybacks, while acknowledging geopolitical, tariff, and brokerage-process risks.

data.title: Northrop Grumman advances Sentinel nuclear missile toward flight test
data.description:
Northrop Grumman (NOC) and the U.S. Air Force assembled a fully integrated inert Sentinel missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base, clearing a key technical milestone ahead of flight testing planned for 2027.

The missile was assembled vertically in its operational orientation during a four-month exercise known as Pathfinder. The demonstration tested whether the program team could transport, handle, stack and integrate the missile safely at a launch site.

 

 

Northrop (NOC) said the exercise included all missile stages, propulsion elements, the protective shroud and related components. Engineers also tested specialized transportation vehicles, mobile crane operations and interfaces on the launch pad.

The inert missile was subsequently taken apart after completion of the exercise.

Design review, flight test schedule

Separately, Northrop Grumman and the Air Force’s 719th Test Squadron completed the first flight-test Critical Design Review.

The review determined that the missile’s design maturity and hardware testing met Air Force requirements for performance, safety and scheduling. The company said Sentinel remains on pace for its first flight test in 2027.

“This vertical assembly demonstrates the momentum toward test launching Sentinel in 2027 and having missiles on alert by the early 2030s,” said Amanda Davis, vice president and general manager of strategic deterrent systems at Northrop Grumman.

The milestones provide evidence that Sentinel is progressing from digital design and component testing toward a physically integrated weapon system. For Northrop (NOC) investors, successful execution is important because Sentinel is expected to remain a major long-duration defense program as the Air Force replaces the aging Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile system.

Northrop (NOC) leads a nationwide Sentinel team of more than 500 suppliers and over 10,000 workers. The planned system is intended to remain operational through 2075, giving the company potential exposure to decades of development, production, maintenance and modernization spending.

The latest achievements do not eliminate the program’s execution risks. Assembling an inert missile demonstrates that its components and ground procedures fit together, but a live flight test will be a more demanding measure of propulsion, guidance, control and overall system performance. Maintaining the 2027 test schedule will therefore be an important milestone for investors monitoring the program.

Modernizing nuclear triad

Sentinel is intended to modernize the land-based portion of the U.S. nuclear triad, which also includes submarine-launched missiles and nuclear-capable aircraft.

Northrop (NOC) said the program is advancing toward initial operational capability in the early 2030s. The company and the Air Force are also working on missile testing, launch infrastructure, supply-chain readiness and the equipment needed to place the weapon in operational silos.

The Pathfinder exercise brings Sentinel closer to that goal, although the program still must complete flight testing and other qualification work before missiles can be placed on alert.
